newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada heavy oil seen out-muscled in U.S. Midwest.
newsitem.headline: Canada heavy oil seen out-muscled in U.S. Midwest.

text.p: Canada's oil production prowess could turn out to be a curse as price competition in the key U.S. Midwest refining market drives down prices for its growing heavy crude oil output.

The market appears set for an extended period of discounting of Canadian heavy crude as rising Canadian volumes compete head-to-head with growing supply from Venezuela, Mexico and elsewhere, analysts said.

Particularly threatening to Canada's oil producers, now faced with a discount of $6 under North American benchmark West Texas Intermediate for their oil compared with $4 or less last year, are Venezuela's large investments in U.S. refining and marketing to secure demand.
"This is the first drop of the glove in terms of what will happen over time to the heavy oil differentials," Martin Molyneaux, analyst with FirstEnergy Capital Corp, said.
"We'll just see how much that market can really take and how aggressive all the sellers want to be."

Canadian heavy oil production growth continues unabated with companies spending hundreds of millions of dollars on drilling and enhanced recovery projects. Between January and September 1996, exports of heavy volumes to the U.S. averaged 556,000 barrels per day, up 8.9 percent from the year before, Statistics Canada figures show.

The ramped up output has coincided with major new additions to pipeline capacity to Midwest refining markets on IPL Energy Inc's Interprovincial Pipe Line system and Express Pipeline, the new Alberta Energy Co Ltd -TransCanada PipeLines Ltd line which moves Canadian oil to southern Illinois via Alberta and Wyoming. Express is within weeks of shipping its full 172,000 barrels per day.
"I think the Canadians are of the mind that 'if you build it, they will come.' Build the pipelines, have new markets and everything will be fine and dandy," said a trader for a large Midwest refiner.

However, refiners have been critical of Canadian producers' lack of interest in securing demand in such ways as shelling out cash for additions to coking capacity, necessary for upgrading the thick, gooey crude.
Venezuela and Mexico, meanwhile, have made major downstream investments in the U.S. over several years.

Players said the difference between the suppliers lies in how their industries are structured. Canada's production is controlled by hundreds of companies which need to boost volumes on a quarterly basis to keep shareholders happy.
Venezuela's and Mexico's output is controlled by state-owned companies, which can take a longer view of making low-return refining investments.
"As a Canadian producer with a C$20-million capital budget, what are you going to do? Take 10 percent of a coker project or drill three dozen wells?" the trader said.
Also, narrow differentials through 1995 and part of 1996 meant it is only in the last six months that adding upgrading capacity has begun to make economic sense, Molyneaux said.

An exception is Suncor Inc, which is mulling deals such as joint ventures, purchases and processing arrangements in the U.S. Midwest that may stem the effects of widening price spreads before the company moves ahead with a major heavy oil project.
But the move bucks the current trend.
"At the moment all the heavy oil projects, as far as we can tell, continue to progress. We'll see if this makes people sit back and think through what they want to do," Molyneaux said.
